clinicalPearls: A benign, encapsulated peripheral nerve sheath tumour of Schwann cells that grows eccentrically and can usually be dissected off the parent nerve
This eccentric, separable growth contrasts with neurofibroma, which is fusiform and entwined with nerve fascicles
Histology shows compact cellular Antoni A areas with nuclear palisading (Verocay bodies) alternating with loose, myxoid Antoni B areas
There is strong, diffuse S100 and SOX10 positivity reflecting Schwann cell origin
Favoured sites include the flexor surfaces of the limbs, the head and neck, spinal nerve roots, and the vestibular nerve, where it forms the vestibular schwannoma
Percussion over the lesion may reproduce paraesthesiae in the nerve distribution, and MRI can show a target sign and a split-fat sign
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2, while multiple non-vestibular tumours suggest schwannomatosis linked to SMARCB1 or LZTR1
Recognised variants include ancient, cellular, plexiform, and melanotic schwannoma, the last associated with Carney complex; malignant change is very rare
reference.pathophysiology: Schwannoma is a benign neoplasm arising from the Schwann cells that form the myelin sheath of peripheral nerves. It grows as a well-encapsulated mass eccentric to the nerve, displacing rather than engulfing the fascicles, which is why it can often be enucleated with preservation of nerve function. Most sporadic tumours show biallelic inactivation of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, whose product merlin normally restrains cell proliferation; loss of merlin function drives Schwann cell overgrowth. Germline NF2 alterations produce neurofibromatosis type 2 with its hallmark bilateral vestibular schwannomas, whereas germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 variants underlie schwannomatosis. Histologically the tumour alternates between organised, cellular Antoni A tissue with palisaded Verocay bodies and hypocellular, myxoid Antoni B tissue, and it characteristically has thick-walled hyalinised vessels. Malignant transformation is exceptional, in contrast to the neurofibroma of neurofibromatosis type 1.
additionalDifferentials: Ganglion cyst adjacent to a nerve
Other soft tissue tumours such as leiomyoma or myxoma
Vestibular schwannoma versus meningioma at the cerebellopontine angle
additionalInvestigations: MRI with contrast to characterise the lesion and its relationship to the nerve, including target and split-fat signs
Audiometry and dedicated internal auditory meatus imaging for suspected vestibular schwannoma
Histology demonstrating Antoni A and B areas with Verocay bodies
Genetic assessment for NF2, SMARCB1, and LZTR1 when multiple tumours or a syndrome is suspected
Nerve conduction studies where functional deficit needs assessment
redFlags: Rapid growth, pain, or new neurological deficit suggesting malignant transformation
Bilateral vestibular tumours or multiple schwannomas indicating an underlying syndrome
Progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, or brainstem compression from a vestibular lesion
Spinal lesions causing cord or root compression
A large deep tumour with atypical imaging features
reference.prognosis: Schwannoma is benign with an excellent prognosis; careful enucleation is usually curative and preserves nerve function, and recurrence is uncommon. Malignant transformation is very rare, and the main determinants of outcome are tumour site and any associated tumour syndrome.
pitfalls: Resecting the nerve unnecessarily when the tumour can be dissected free with preservation of function
Overinterpreting the degenerative atypia of ancient schwannoma as malignancy
Failing to investigate for neurofibromatosis type 2 or schwannomatosis when tumours are multiple or bilateral
Confusing schwannoma with neurofibroma and thereby misjudging the risk of malignant transformation

management: Offer observation with serial imaging for small, asymptomatic tumours given their benign, slow-growing nature
Treat symptomatic or enlarging lesions by microsurgical enucleation, dissecting the tumour off the parent nerve to preserve nerve function
For vestibular schwannoma choose between surveillance, microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery according to size, hearing and symptoms
Provide symptomatic management of pain and neurological deficit, with nerve-conduction assessment where function is impaired
Undertake genetic evaluation for NF2, SMARCB1 or LZTR1 when tumours are multiple or a syndrome is suspected, and screen accordingly
Refer for specialist neurosurgical, skull-base or soft-tissue multidisciplinary input
Reassure regarding the excellent prognosis, as malignant transformation is very rare and enucleation is usually curative
